question: What is the maximum rate of echolocation pulses produced by bats during the terminal buzz?
ground_truth: During the terminal buzz some bats can produce echolocation clicks at rates of up to 200 clicks per second.
answer: During the terminal buzz, echolocating bats produce pulses at rates as high as 200 clicks per second [Source: bat-echolocation.txt].
contexts:
Echolocating bats generate ultrasound via the larynx and emit the sound through the open mouth or, much more rarely, the nose.

When searching for prey, bats produce sounds at a low rate of 10 to 20 clicks per second. During the search phase, the sound emission is coupled to respiration, which is again coupled to the wingbeat. After detecting a potential prey item, echolocating bats increase the rate of pulses, ending with the terminal buzz at rates as high as 200 clicks per second. During approach to a detected target, the duration of the sounds is gradually decreased, as is the energy of the sound.

Bat echolocation calls range in frequency from 14,000 to well over 100,000 Hz, mostly beyond the range of the human ear. Typical human hearing range is considered to be from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Bat call frequencies range from as low as 11 kHz to as high as 212 kHz. Insectivorous aerial-hawking bats, those that chase prey in the open air, have a call frequency between 20 kHz and 60 kHz, because it is the frequency that gives the best range and image acuity and makes them less conspicuous to insects. High-intensity calls such as those from aerial-hawking bats reach 133 dB. Their high intensity calls are necessary to have moderate detection of surroundings because air has a high absorption of ultrasound and because insects' size provides only a small target for sound reflection.

The time interval between subsequent echolocation calls determines two aspects of a bat's perception. First, it establishes how quickly the bat's auditory scene information is updated. Bats increase the repetition rate of their calls as they home in on a target, allowing new information about the target's location to arrive at a faster rate when it is needed most. Secondly, the pulse interval determines the maximum range at which bats can detect objects. Bats can only keep track of the echoes from one call at a time; as soon as they make another call, they stop listening for echoes from the previously made call. A pulse interval of 100 milliseconds (typical of a bat searching for insects) allows sound to travel roughly 34 metres, so a bat can only detect objects as far away as 17 metres. With a pulse interval of 5 milliseconds (typical of a bat in the final moments of a capture attempt), the bat can only detect objects up to 85 centimetres away.

A single echolocation call can last anywhere from less than 3 to over 50 milliseconds in duration. Reducing duration comes at the cost of having less total sound available for reflecting off objects and being heard by the bat.

Bats can inadvertently jam each other with their echolocation calls. To avoid this, individual bat species echolocate within specific frequency ranges that suit their environment and prey types. In some situations, bats may stop calling altogether or shift their call frequency to avoid jamming from neighbours using the same frequency range.

Both CF and FM bats have specialised inner ears which allow them to hear sounds in the ultrasonic range, far outside the range of human hearing. In bats that use a constant frequency component, there is a disproportionately large section of the basilar membrane that responds to the specific frequency of the bat's returning echoes. This area of high sensitivity to a narrow range of frequency is known as an "acoustic fovea." Echolocating bats also have cochlear hair cells that are especially resistant to intense noise — a necessary adaptation given the intensity of their own calls.

Additionally, the so-called "whispering bats" have adapted low-amplitude echolocation so that their prey, moths that are able to hear echolocation calls, are less able to detect and avoid an oncoming bat.

Unlike some human-made sonars that rely on many extremely narrow beams and many receivers to localise a target, animal echolocation has only one transmitter and two receivers (the ears) positioned slightly apart. The echoes returning to the ears arrive at different times and at different intensities, depending on the position of the object generating the echoes. The time and loudness differences are used by the animals to perceive distance and direction. With echolocation, the bat or other animal can determine not only where it is going, but also how big another animal is, what kind of animal it is, and other features.

Their use of echolocation, along with powered flight, allows them to occupy a niche where there are often many insects that come out at night, less competition for food, and fewer species that may prey on the bats themselves.

question: How do honey bees encode the distance to a food source?
ground_truth: Honey bees encode distance to a food source through the duration of the waggle run in the waggle dance. A longer waggle run indicates a more distant food source.
answer: The distance between the hive and a recruitment target is encoded in the duration of the waggle runs. The farther the target, the longer the waggle phase [Source: bee-communication.txt].
contexts:
The waggle dance is beneficial in some environments and not in others. Depending on weather, other competitors, and food source characteristics, transmitted information may quickly degrade and become obsolete. The waggle dance plays a significantly larger role in foraging when food sources are not as abundant. In tropical habitats, honey bee foraging is severely impaired if waggle dancing is prevented, whereas in temperate habitats colonies were still able to successfully forage when the location information provided by the dance was experimentally obscured. This difference is thought to be due to the patchiness of resources in tropical environments versus the homogeneity of resources in temperate environments.

Observations have suggested that different species of honeybees have different "dialects" of the waggle dance, each species or subspecies dance varying by curve or duration. A study from 2008 demonstrated that a mixed colony of Asiatic honeybees and European honeybees were gradually able to understand one another's dialects of waggle dance.

Kevin Abbott and Reuven Dukas discovered that if a dead western honeybee is placed on a flower, bees performed far fewer waggle dances upon returning to the hive. The scientists explain that the bees associate the dead bee with the presence of a predator at the food source. The reduction of the dance repetition frequency indicates that the dancing bees perform and communicate a form of risk/benefit analysis.

If multiple bees are doing the waggle dance, it is a competition to convince the observing bees to follow their lead, and competing bees may even disrupt other bees' dances or fight each other off.

Waggle-dancing bees produce and release two alkanes, tricosane and pentacosane, and two alkenes onto their abdomens and into the air. Honeybees accumulate an electric charge during flying and when their body parts are moved or rubbed together. Bees emit constant and modulated electric fields during the waggle dance. Both low- and high-frequency components emitted by dancing bees induce passive antennal movements in stationary bees. Recordings from axons of the Johnston's organ indicate its sensitivity to electric fields. Therefore, it has been suggested that electric fields emanating from the surface charge of bees stimulate mechanoreceptors and may play a role in social communication during the waggle dance.

Waggle-dancing bees that have been in the nest for an extended time adjust the angles of their dances to accommodate the changing direction of the sun. Therefore, bees that follow the waggle run of the dance are still correctly led to the food source even though its angle relative to the sun has changed.

As defined by von Frisch, Tanzsprache (German for "dance language") is the information about direction, distance, and quality of a resource contained within the waggle dance.

Austrian ethologist and Nobel laureate Karl von Frisch was one of the first who translated the meaning of the waggle dance.

A waggle dance consists of one to 100 or more circuits, each of which consists of two phases: the waggle phase and the return phase. A worker bee's waggle dance involves running through a small figure-eight pattern: a waggle run followed by a turn to the right to circle back to the starting point, another waggle run, followed by a turn and circle to the left, and so on in a regular alternation between right and left turns after waggle runs.

The direction and duration of waggle runs are closely correlated with the direction and distance of the resource being advertised by the dancing bee. For cavity-nesting honey bees, like the western honey bee (Apis mellifera), flowers that are located directly in line with the sun are represented by waggle runs in an upward direction on the vertical combs, and any angle to the right or left of the sun is coded by a corresponding angle to the right or left of the upward direction. The distance between hive and recruitment target is encoded in the duration of the waggle runs. The farther the target, the longer the waggle phase. The more excited the bee is about the location, the more rapidly it will waggle, so it will grab the attention of the observing bees.

As defined by von Frisch, Tanzsprache (German for "dance language") is the information about direction, distance, and quality of a resource contained within the waggle dance.

The waggle dance may be less efficient than once thought. Some bees observe over 50 waggle runs without successfully foraging, while others will forage successfully after observing 5 runs. Studies have found that honeybees rarely make use of the information communicated in the waggle dance and seem to only do so about ten percent of the time. There can be a conflict between private information based upon individual experiences, and social information transmitted through dance communication. Foragers often prefer to use remembered information about previously rewarding food sites that they have visited and will use this information even when receiving dance information about new food sources.

question: What percentage of a coral's energy needs can zooxanthellae provide through photosynthesis?
ground_truth: Zooxanthellae can provide up to 90 percent of a coral's energy needs through photosynthesis.
answer: Zooxanthellae can provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy needs through products of photosynthesis [Source: coral-reefs.txt].
contexts:
The corals that form the great reef ecosystems of tropical seas depend upon a symbiotic relationship with algae-like single-celled flagellate protozoa called zooxanthellae that live within their tissues and give the coral its coloration. The zooxanthellae provide the coral with nutrients through photosynthesis, a crucial factor in the clear and nutrient-poor tropical waters. As the zooxanthellae provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy needs through products of photosynthesis, the health of the coral depends entirely on the health of this symbiotic relationship. In exchange, the coral provides the zooxanthellae with the carbon dioxide and ammonium needed for photosynthesis.

Coral bleaching is the process where corals become white due to loss of their symbiotic algae and photosynthetic pigments. This loss of pigment can be caused by various stressors, such as changes in water temperature, light, salinity, or nutrients. A bleached coral is under stress, more vulnerable to starvation and disease, and at risk of death. The leading cause of coral bleaching is rising ocean temperatures due to climate change.

Coral can survive short-term disturbances, but if the conditions that lead to the expulsion of the zooxanthellae persist, the coral's chances of survival diminish. In order to recover from bleaching, the zooxanthellae have to re-enter the tissues of the coral polyps and restart photosynthesis. If the coral polyps die of starvation after bleaching, they will decay. The hard coral species will then leave behind their calcium carbonate skeletons, which will be taken over by algae, effectively blocking coral regrowth. Eventually, the coral skeletons will erode, causing the reef structure to collapse. While it can take 10 to 15 years to restore damaged and bleached coral reefs, many reefs face repeated bleaching before they can recover.

Reefs either recover from bleaching, where they are recolonised by zooxanthellae, or they experience a regime shift, where previously flourishing coral reefs are taken over by thick layers of macroalgae. This inhibits further coral growth because the algae produces antifouling compounds to deter settlement and competes with corals for space and light.

Species of coral that can increase their carnivorous tendencies have been found to have an increased likelihood of recovering from bleaching events, since they can find alternative sources of energy while waiting for zooxanthellae to return. This variation in resilience across coral species is one reason some reefs fare better than others under the same thermal stress.

A coral reef is a large underwater structure made of dead and living corals. In most healthy reefs, stony corals are predominant. They are built from colonial polyps from the phylum Cnidaria which secrete an exoskeleton of calcium carbonate. The reefs are formed in tropical marine areas and act as the home of many tropical fish and other animals.

Most present-day coral reefs were formed after the last ice age when melting ice caused the sea level to rise and flood the continental shelves. As coral reef communities were established on the shelves, they built reefs that grew upwards, keeping pace with the rise in sea level. Reefs that did not keep pace became drowned reefs, covered by so much water that there was insufficient light for further survival.

question: What temperature can water emerging from hydrothermal vents reach?
ground_truth: Water emerging from hydrothermal vents can range from about 60°C to as high as 464°C.
answer: Water emerging from hydrothermal vents can reach temperatures ranging from 60 degrees Celsius up to as high as 464 degrees Celsius [Source: deep-sea-vents.txt].
contexts:
In contrast to the approximately 2 degrees Celsius ambient water temperature at these depths, water emerges from these vents at temperatures ranging from 60 degrees Celsius up to as high as 464 degrees Celsius. Due to the high hydrostatic pressure at these depths, water may exist in either its liquid form or as a supercritical fluid at such temperatures.

A black smoker or deep-sea vent is a type of hydrothermal vent found on the seabed, typically in the bathyal zone at depths from 2,500 to 3,000 metres. They appear as black, chimney-like structures that emit a cloud of black material. Black smokers are formed in fields hundreds of metres wide when superheated water from below Earth's crust comes through the ocean floor. This water is rich in dissolved minerals from the crust, most notably sulfides. When it comes in contact with cold ocean water, many minerals precipitate, forming a black, chimney-like structure around each vent. Some of these chimney structures can reach heights of 60 metres.

White smoker vents emit lighter-hued minerals, such as those containing barium, calcium, and silicon. These vents also tend to have lower-temperature plumes, probably because they are generally more distant from their heat source.

Hydrothermal vents are fissures on the seabed from which geothermally heated water discharges. They are commonly found near volcanically active places, areas where tectonic plates are moving apart at mid-ocean ridges, ocean basins, and hotspots. The dispersal of hydrothermal fluids throughout the global ocean at active vent sites creates hydrothermal plumes.

Hydrothermal vents exist because the Earth is both geologically active and has large amounts of water on its surface and within its crust. Under the sea, they may form features called black smokers or white smokers, which deliver a wide range of elements to the world's oceans, thus contributing to global marine biogeochemistry. Relative to the majority of the deep sea, the areas around hydrothermal vents are biologically more productive, often hosting complex communities fueled by the chemicals dissolved in the vent fluids. Chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea found around hydrothermal vents form the base of the food chain, supporting diverse organisms including giant tube worms, clams, limpets, and shrimp.

Hydrothermal vents have been hypothesised to have been a significant factor in starting abiogenesis and the survival of primitive life. The chemical and thermal dynamics in hydrothermal vents make such environments thermodynamically suitable for chemical evolution processes. Some researchers have proposed that the earliest life on Earth may have originated in conditions similar to those found at deep-sea alkaline hydrothermal vents, where naturally occurring proton gradients could have driven the earliest metabolic reactions.

White smoker vents emit lighter-hued minerals, such as those containing barium, calcium, and silicon. These vents also tend to have lower-temperature plumes, probably because they are generally more distant from their heat source.

Life has traditionally been seen as driven by energy from the sun, but deep-sea organisms have no access to sunlight, so biological communities around hydrothermal vents must depend on nutrients found in the chemical deposits and hydrothermal fluids in which they live. Hydrothermal vents are recognised as a type of chemosynthetic-based ecosystem where primary productivity is fuelled by chemical compounds as energy sources instead of light. Hydrothermal vent communities are able to sustain such vast amounts of life because vent organisms depend on chemosynthetic bacteria for food. The water from the hydrothermal vent is rich in dissolved minerals and supports a large population of chemoautotrophic bacteria. These bacteria use sulfur compounds, particularly hydrogen sulfide, a chemical highly toxic to most known organisms, to produce organic material through the process of chemosynthesis. Compared to the surrounding sea floor, hydrothermal vent zones have a density of organisms 10,000 to 100,000 times greater.

Hydrothermal vents are fissures on the seabed from which geothermally heated water discharges. They are commonly found near volcanically active places, areas where tectonic plates are moving apart at mid-ocean ridges, ocean basins, and hotspots. The dispersal of hydrothermal fluids throughout the global ocean at active vent sites creates hydrothermal plumes.

Hydrothermal vents exist because the Earth is both geologically active and has large amounts of water on its surface and within its crust. Under the sea, they may form features called black smokers or white smokers, which deliver a wide range of elements to the world's oceans, thus contributing to global marine biogeochemistry. Relative to the majority of the deep sea, the areas around hydrothermal vents are biologically more productive, often hosting complex communities fueled by the chemicals dissolved in the vent fluids. Chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea found around hydrothermal vents form the base of the food chain, supporting diverse organisms including giant tube worms, clams, limpets, and shrimp.

In contrast to the approximately 2 degrees Celsius ambient water temperature at these depths, water emerges from these vents at temperatures ranging from 60 degrees Celsius up to as high as 464 degrees Celsius. Due to the high hydrostatic pressure at these depths, water may exist in either its liquid form or as a supercritical fluid at such temperatures.

A black smoker or deep-sea vent is a type of hydrothermal vent found on the seabed, typically in the bathyal zone at depths from 2,500 to 3,000 metres. They appear as black, chimney-like structures that emit a cloud of black material. Black smokers are formed in fields hundreds of metres wide when superheated water from below Earth's crust comes through the ocean floor. This water is rich in dissolved minerals from the crust, most notably sulfides. When it comes in contact with cold ocean water, many minerals precipitate, forming a black, chimney-like structure around each vent. Some of these chimney structures can reach heights of 60 metres.

White smoker vents emit lighter-hued minerals, such as those containing barium, calcium, and silicon. These vents also tend to have lower-temperature plumes, probably because they are generally more distant from their heat source.

Hydrothermal vents have been hypothesised to have been a significant factor in starting abiogenesis and the survival of primitive life. The chemical and thermal dynamics in hydrothermal vents make such environments thermodynamically suitable for chemical evolution processes. Some researchers have proposed that the earliest life on Earth may have originated in conditions similar to those found at deep-sea alkaline hydrothermal vents, where naturally occurring proton gradients could have driven the earliest metabolic reactions.

In 1977, scientists from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography obtained the first evidence for submarine hydrothermal vents along the Galapagos Rift. The chemosynthetic ecosystems surrounding the vents were first directly observed on 17 February 1977, when a group of marine geologists returned to the Clambake sites aboard the submersible DSV Alvin. The Pompeii worm Alvinella pompejana, which is capable of withstanding temperatures up to 80 degrees Celsius, was found in the 1980s. The scaly-foot gastropod was first found in 2001 and uses iron sulfides for the structure of its hardened body parts, instead of calcium carbonate — an adaptation unique among known animals.

A coral reef is a large underwater structure made of dead and living corals. In most healthy reefs, stony corals are predominant. They are built from colonial polyps from the phylum Cnidaria which secrete an exoskeleton of calcium carbonate. The reefs are formed in tropical marine areas and act as the home of many tropical fish and other animals.

Most present-day coral reefs were formed after the last ice age when melting ice caused the sea level to rise and flood the continental shelves. As coral reef communities were established on the shelves, they built reefs that grew upwards, keeping pace with the rise in sea level. Reefs that did not keep pace became drowned reefs, covered by so much water that there was insufficient light for further survival.

Coral can survive short-term disturbances, but if the conditions that lead to the expulsion of the zooxanthellae persist, the coral's chances of survival diminish. This inhibits further coral growth because the algae produces antifouling compounds to deter settlement and competes with corals for space and light.

Unlike some human-made sonars that rely on many extremely narrow beams and many receivers to localise a target, animal echolocation has only one transmitter and two receivers (the ears) positioned slightly apart. With echolocation, the bat or other animal can determine not only where it is going, but also how big another animal is, what kind of animal it is, and other features.

Echolocating bats use echolocation to navigate and forage, often in total darkness. They generally emerge from their roosts in caves, attics, or trees at dusk and hunt for insects into the night. Using echolocation, bats can determine how far away an object is, the object's size, shape and density, and the direction that an object is moving. Their use of echolocation, along with powered flight, allows them to occupy a niche where there are often many insects that come out at night, less competition for food, and fewer species that may prey on the bats themselves.

Echolocating bats generate ultrasound via the larynx and emit the sound through the open mouth or, much more rarely, the nose.

When searching for prey, bats produce sounds at a low rate of 10 to 20 clicks per second. During the search phase, the sound emission is coupled to respiration, which is again coupled to the wingbeat. After detecting a potential prey item, echolocating bats increase the rate of pulses, ending with the terminal buzz at rates as high as 200 clicks per second. During approach to a detected target, the duration of the sounds is gradually decreased, as is the energy of the sound.

Bat echolocation calls range in frequency from 14,000 to well over 100,000 Hz, mostly beyond the range of the human ear. Typical human hearing range is considered to be from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Bat call frequencies range from as low as 11 kHz to as high as 212 kHz. Insectivorous aerial-hawking bats, those that chase prey in the open air, have a call frequency between 20 kHz and 60 kHz, because it is the frequency that gives the best range and image acuity and makes them less conspicuous to insects. High-intensity calls such as those from aerial-hawking bats reach 133 dB. Their high intensity calls are necessary to have moderate detection of surroundings because air has a high absorption of ultrasound and because insects' size provides only a small target for sound reflection.

Bats can inadvertently jam each other with their echolocation calls. To avoid this, individual bat species echolocate within specific frequency ranges that suit their environment and prey types. In some situations, bats may stop calling altogether or shift their call frequency to avoid jamming from neighbours using the same frequency range.

Both CF and FM bats have specialised inner ears which allow them to hear sounds in the ultrasonic range, far outside the range of human hearing. In bats that use a constant frequency component, there is a disproportionately large section of the basilar membrane that responds to the specific frequency of the bat's returning echoes. This area of high sensitivity to a narrow range of frequency is known as an "acoustic fovea." Echolocating bats also have cochlear hair cells that are especially resistant to intense noise — a necessary adaptation given the intensity of their own calls.

Additionally, the so-called "whispering bats" have adapted low-amplitude echolocation so that their prey, moths that are able to hear echolocation calls, are less able to detect and avoid an oncoming bat.

The time interval between subsequent echolocation calls determines two aspects of a bat's perception. First, it establishes how quickly the bat's auditory scene information is updated. Bats increase the repetition rate of their calls as they home in on a target, allowing new information about the target's location to arrive at a faster rate when it is needed most. Secondly, the pulse interval determines the maximum range at which bats can detect objects. Bats can only keep track of the echoes from one call at a time; as soon as they make another call, they stop listening for echoes from the previously made call. A pulse interval of 100 milliseconds (typical of a bat searching for insects) allows sound to travel roughly 34 metres, so a bat can only detect objects as far away as 17 metres. With a pulse interval of 5 milliseconds (typical of a bat in the final moments of a capture attempt), the bat can only detect objects up to 85 centimetres away.

A single echolocation call can last anywhere from less than 3 to over 50 milliseconds in duration. Reducing duration comes at the cost of having less total sound available for reflecting off objects and being heard by the bat.
